title: Photography basics
examples: What is the difference between aperture and shutter speed?
How does the rule of thirds make a photo look better?
When should I use a fast shutter speed?

explain.say: Today we are learning about photography basics. We will look at how to make your pictures look professional.

draw.text: Photography Basics: Exposure, Rule of Thirds, Light

explain.say: First we look at the exposure triangle. This controls how bright your photo is.

draw.text: Exposure Triangle: Aperture, Shutter Speed, ISO

explain.say: Aperture controls the amount of light entering the lens. A smaller number means a wider opening.
Shutter speed controls how long the camera sensor sees the light. A fast speed freezes motion.

draw.text: Shutter Speed: Freezes or blurs motion

explain.say: ISO controls the camera's sensitivity to light. Higher ISO numbers are for darker places.
Next we look at the rule of thirds. Imagine dividing your picture into nine equal parts.

draw.text: Rule of Thirds: Nine equal parts

faq.a: Aperture controls the size of the opening in your camera lens. This opening lets different amounts of light reach the sensor.
asks: How big is the lens opening?

faq.q: When should I use a fast shutter speed?
faq.a: You should use a fast shutter speed when you want to freeze fast action, like a jumping animal. This keeps the picture sharp.
asks: How do I stop motion in photos?

faq.q: What is the rule of thirds about?
faq.a: It is a guideline for placing important things in your photo. You should try to put subjects along the lines or at the intersections.
asks: How do I compose a picture well?
Where should I place my subject?

faq.a: Yes, light is everything in photography. The quality and direction of light change how your subject looks entirely.
asks: What is good light for pictures?

faq.q: Can I use high ISO all the time?
faq.a: No, using high ISO too much can make your photos look grainy or noisy. Use it only when you have very little light.
asks: When is high ISO okay to use?

facts: The exposure triangle links aperture, shutter speed, and ISO.
The rule of thirds suggests placing subjects on intersecting lines.
Aperture size is often measured using f-numbers.
Low light conditions usually require a higher ISO setting.

quiz.say: To make a photo of a running dog look frozen in time, which setting should you use?
quiz.show: Freezing motion requires a fast shutter speed.
quiz.why: A fast shutter speed closes the sensor quickly, capturing the dog at one exact moment.

wrong.0: A small aperture controls light, not the speed of the shutter.
wrong.1: High ISO increases sensitivity, but does not stop movement.
wrong.2: This is a composition guide, not a technical setting.

quiz.say: If you want to make a portrait where the background is blurry, which setting is best?
quiz.show: Blurry background needs a wide aperture.
quiz.why: A wide aperture lets in a lot of light and creates a shallow depth of field, blurring the background.

wrong.0: Low ISO only affects the sensor's sensitivity to light.
wrong.2: A narrow aperture keeps everything in focus, making the background clear.
wrong.3: Slow shutter speed blurs movement, not just the background.

quiz.say: When composing a picture of a mountain range, where is the strongest placement according to the rule of thirds?
quiz.show: Mountain range on the top line.

options.show: Along one of the intersecting lines
options.say: Along one of the intersecting lines

quiz.why: The rule suggests placing key elements along the lines or at the intersections of the imaginary grid.

wrong.0: While sometimes necessary, this ignores the compositional guidelines.
wrong.1: The rule of thirds applies to all thirds, not just the bottom one.
wrong.3: Placing everything in the center can make the photo feel static or boring.
